main: Dabao = Baochip-1x dev board (Pico-style footprint, 3.3 V logic)
sub: Goal: let a Kakute flight controller and the Dabao exchange data over a serial (UART) link.
say: This is the Dabao, a small development board built around the Baochip one X RISC-V chip. The goal is to let a Kakute flight controller and the Dabao talk to each other over a serial link, so the flight controller can stream data to the Dabao, and the Dabao can send results or commands back.

main: GND · VSYS (5 V in) · PB13 UART2_RX · PB14 UART2_TX
sub: UART2 is the only serial port brought out on the Dabao header. Everything else stays free.
say: We only need four of its pins. Ground, VSYS for power, and the UART2 pair: PB13, which receives, and PB14, which transmits. UART2 is the only serial port brought out on the Dabao header, so that's the one we'll use.

step: Your Mac · 1 of 4 · Flash the Dabao
main: Mac USB-C  →  Dabao USB port
sub: Press RESET, then:  ./bao_flash.sh flash /dev/cu.usbmodemXXXX my_app   (ls /dev/cu.* shows the port)
say: Before any wiring, set up each board on its own from your Mac. First, plug the Dabao into your Mac with a USB C cable. Press reset, and it shows up as a USB modem serial port. Use the bao flash script from the SDK to build and flash your program. This USB link is only for programming.

step: Your Mac · 2 of 4 · Optional: watch the Dabao's output
main: 3.3 V USB-serial adapter  →  Dabao PB13 / PB14 / GND
sub: Adapter TX → PB13 · Adapter RX ← PB14 · GND → GND · then:  .venv/bin/pyserial-miniterm /dev/cu.usbserial-XXXX 115200
say: Optionally, to see what your program prints, connect a 3.3 volt USB to serial adapter. Adapter transmit goes to PB13, adapter receive goes to PB14, and ground to ground. Open a serial terminal at 115200 baud. Because the flight controller will use these same two pins, this is a bench test only. Remove the adapter before wiring the flight controller.

step: Your Mac · 3 of 4 · Configure the flight controller
main: Mac  →  Kakute USB   (H743-Wing: USB dongle · H7 V1.5: on-board USB-C)
sub: QGroundControl / Mission Planner (ArduPilot) or Betaflight / INAV Configurator → set the UART to 115200 baud.
say: Next, connect the Kakute to your Mac. The H743 Wing uses its small USB dongle on a six pin cable. The H7 version 1.5 has a USB C port on the board. Open your ground station, QGroundControl for ArduPilot, or the Betaflight or INAV configurator, and set the serial port we're about to wire to 115200 baud.

step: Your Mac · 4 of 4 · Unplug the Dabao
main: Disconnect the Dabao's USB cable and the adapter
sub: From here on, the flight controller powers the Dabao. Two power sources at once can back-feed each other.
say: When both boards are programmed and configured, unplug the Dabao's USB cable and the adapter. From now on the flight controller powers the Dabao, and powering it from two sources at once could back feed one supply into the other.

main: Using UART2 — pads T2 and R2
sub: UART1 = GPS port, UART6 = RC receiver input. UART2 (TELEM2) is normally free.
say: Now the Kakute H743 Wing. We'll use UART2, the pads marked T2 and R2. On this board UART1 is the GPS port and UART6 is the receiver input, while UART2, telemetry two, is normally free.

main: FC “G” pad  →  Dabao GND (left column, row 13)
sub: A shared ground is the reference every signal voltage is measured against.
say: Step one, ground. Solder a wire from the G pad to any Dabao ground pin. A serial signal is just a voltage measured against ground, so both boards need the same ground reference, or the data is meaningless.

main: FC “5V” pad  →  Dabao VSYS (right column, row 2 · pin 39)
sub: VSYS is the Dabao's main power input; its regulator makes 3.3 V. Never put 5 V on any other Dabao pin.
say: Step two, power. The flight controller's 5 volt pad goes to VSYS on the Dabao. VSYS is the board's main power input, and its regulator makes the 3.3 volts the chip needs. Now the Dabao switches on whenever the drone's battery is connected. Never put 5 volts on any other Dabao pin.

step: Step 3 of 4 · FC transmit → Dabao receive
main: FC “T2”  →  Dabao PB13 (UART2_RX · pin 16)
sub: TX always goes to RX — the lines are crossed, never TX-to-TX.
say: Step three. T2 is the flight controller's transmit line. It goes to PB13, the Dabao's receive pin. One board's mouth goes to the other board's ear, so transmit always connects to receive.

step: Step 4 of 4 · Dabao transmit → FC receive
main: Dabao PB14 (UART2_TX · pin 15)  →  FC “R2”
sub: Both boards use 3.3 V logic, so no level shifter is needed.
say: Step four. PB14, the Dabao's transmit pin, goes to R2, the flight controller's receive pad. Now data flows both ways. Both boards use 3.3 volt logic, so no level shifter is needed.

main: Kakute H743-Wing ↔ Dabao is wired
sub: ArduPilot: SERIAL2_BAUD = 115, SERIAL2_PROTOCOL = what your Dabao program speaks (e.g. 2 = MAVLink2).
say: That's it. Yellow dots show data from the flight controller to the Dabao, and blue dots show data coming back. In ArduPilot, UART2 is SERIAL2. Set SERIAL2 baud to 115, and set the protocol to whatever your Dabao program speaks, for example MAVLink 2.

main: Same wiring — but on UART4, pads T4 and R4
sub: T1/R1 and R6 sit on the VTX plug, UART3 is usually GPS, so UART4 is the free one.
say: The Kakute H7 version 1.5 is wired the same way. The difference is the port. UART1 and UART6 are on the video transmitter plug, and UART3 is usually the GPS, so we use UART4, pads T4 and R4.

main: FC “G” pad  →  Dabao GND
sub: Common ground first.
say: Ground first. The G pad goes to a Dabao ground pin, so both boards share one reference.

main: FC “5V” pad  →  Dabao VSYS
sub: The flight controller now powers the Dabao.
say: Then the 5 volt pad goes to VSYS, so the flight controller powers the Dabao.

step: Step 3 of 4 · FC transmit → Dabao receive
main: FC “T4”  →  Dabao PB13 (RX)
sub: Transmit to receive.
say: T4, the flight controller's transmit, goes to PB13, the Dabao's receive.

step: Step 4 of 4 · Dabao transmit → FC receive
main: Dabao PB14 (TX)  →  FC “R4”
sub: And back the other way.
say: And PB14, the Dabao's transmit, goes to R4, the flight controller's receive.

main: Kakute H7 V1.5 ↔ Dabao is wired
sub: ArduPilot: SERIAL4_BAUD = 115, SERIAL4_PROTOCOL = what your Dabao program speaks.
say: Done. In ArduPilot, UART4 is SERIAL4, so set SERIAL4 baud to 115, and pick the protocol your Dabao program uses. Take a moment to see it from every side.

main: Same 4 wires on both boards
sub: GND → GND · 5V → VSYS · FC TX → PB13 · PB14 → FC RX
say: To recap. Ground to ground, 5 volts to VSYS, flight controller transmit to PB13, and PB14 to flight controller receive. Flash the Dabao over USB first, use the serial adapter only on the bench, and unplug both before connecting the flight controller.

main: Battery in → FC USB to Mac → watch the UART in your ground station
sub: If nothing arrives: check TX/RX aren't swapped, the baud rates match, and the grounds are joined.
say: Finally, connect the battery, plug the flight controller into your Mac, and check in your ground station that data from the Dabao is arriving. If nothing shows up, check that transmit and receive aren't swapped, the baud rates match, and the grounds are joined.
